swoop.e: From Middle English swopen, from Old English swāpan (“to sweep”). Doublet of swaip. See also sweep, which was probably the basis for analogical restoration of /w/ in this word.

d.g: To move with a rushing or swirling sound
d.x: The fishing rod swooshed through the air.

d.g: A swooshing movement or sound
d.x: "What the hell is a swoosh?" the McDonald's rep asked. "You know — a swoosh. Like when you go fast. 'Swoosh!'"

d.g: A pattern or logo suggesting a swooshing movement.
d.x: Even TV announcers at the last Winter Olympics were spotted with a swoosh on their jackets.

d.g: Alternative spelling of swap.
Alternative spelling of swap.
d.x: 'We make a pair, by God and by St James! / But, brother, what do you say to swopping names?'

d.g: A fusion of swing and hip-hop dance styles.
A long bladed weapon with a grip and typically a pommel and crossguard (together forming a hilt), which is designed to cut, stab, slash and/or hack.
d.x: He took out his sword and stabbed the man in the stomach.

d.g: A suit in certain playing card decks, particularly those used in Spain and Italy, or those used for divination.
A card of this suit.
One of the end bars by which the lay of a hand loom is suspended.

sword.e: Inherited from West Midland Middle English sword (swerd in most dialects), from Old English sweord (“sword”), from Proto-West Germanic *swerd (“sword”), from Proto-Germanic *swerdą (“sword”), possibly from Proto-Indo-European *seh₂w- (“sharp”). …

d.g: A large marine fish with a long, pointed bill, Xiphias gladius.
d.x: One reason, the department suggested, was that affluent New Yorkers were likely to eat expensive fish high in mercury, like swordfish and tuna.

d.g: A sudoku technique involving possible cell locations for a digit, or pair, or triple, in uniquely three rows and three columns only. This allows for the elimination of candidates around the grid.
To fish for swordfish.

swordfish.e: From Middle English swerdfysche, from Old English *sweordfisċ. Equivalent to sword + fish.

d.g: fighting with a sword
d.x: His expertise at swordplay made his acting in the part of Hamlet very believable.

swordplay.e: Inherited from Old English sweordplega. By surface analysis, sword + play.

d.g: A person skilled at using swords in sport or combat; a fencer.
d.x: He is a remarkable swordsman.

d.g: A person who fights with a sword.
d.x: Archers attempted to take down an unknown swordsman.

d.g: A man who is a skillful or enthusiastic practitioner of sexual intercourse.
d.x: Jennifer Aniston is in control . . . and getting what she needs from a notorious swordsman eight years her junior.

swordsman.e: English sword English -s- Proto-Indo-European *mon- Proto-Germanic *mann- Proto-West Germanic *mann Old English mann Middle English man English man English swordsman From sword + -s- + man.

d.g: the skill of using a sword

swordsmanship.e: English swordsman Proto-Germanic *skapjaną Proto-Germanic *-skapiz Proto-West Germanic *-skapi Old English -sċiepe Middle English -schipe English -ship English swordsmanship From swordsman + -ship.

d.g: One of many species of freshwater fish, in genus Xiphophorus, others of which are called platyfish.

d.g: Any of various papilionid butterflies that have a long sword-like projection from the tornal section of each hindwing.
To study with effort or determination.

d.g: One who swots; a boffin, nerd, or smart aleck.
d.x: On first listen, Americans of a certain vintage would call one a Poindexter, while older Brits would regard the other as a swot.

d.g: Work.

d.g: Vigorous study at an educational institution.

swot.e: From a dialectal English word, from Middle English swot, swat, from Old English swāt (“perspiration; sweat”), from Proto-Germanic *swaitą (“sweat”). More at sweat.

d.g: To bind (a baby) with long narrow strips of cloth.
Anything used to swaddle with, such as a cloth or band.
d.x: They put me in bed in all my swaddles.

swaddle.e: From Middle English swathlen (“to bind; swaddle”), from Middle English swathel, swethel, from Old English swaþul, swæþel, sweþel, sweoþol (“swaddling cloth”), equivalent to swathe (“to wrap with fabric”) + -le (agent/instrumental suffix), the word then underwent th-stopping (its voiced th became a d). …

d.g: To take an oath, to promise intensely, solemnly, and/or with legally binding effect.
d.x: The knight swore not to return to the palace until he had found the treasure.

d.g: To take an oath that an assertion is true.
d.x: The witness swore that the person she had seen running out of the bank was a foot shorter than the accused.

d.g: To promise intensely that something is true; to strongly assert.
d.x: I swear I don't know what you're talking about.

d.g: To administer an oath to (a person).
d.x: Let the witness be sworn.

swear.e: From Middle English sweren, swerien, from Old English swerian (“to swear, take an oath of office”), from Proto-West Germanic *swarjan, from Proto-Germanic *swarjaną (“to speak, swear”), from Proto-Indo-European *swer- (“to swear”). …

d.g: To make sweet to the taste.

d.g: To make (more) pleasant or to the mind or feelings.

d.g: To make mild or kind; to soften.
d.x: to sweeten the temper

d.g: To make less painful or laborious; to relieve.

sweeten.e: From sweet + -en. Eclipsed non-native Middle English doucen and endoucen, borrowed from Old French adoucir and endoucir (“to sweeten”).

d.g: To suffer terribly from intense heat.
To perspire greatly from heat.
To cause to faint, to overpower, as with heat.

It was so rare a piece of fun
To see the swelter'd cattle run

d.g: Intense heat.
d.x: The summer swelter did not relent until late in September, most years.

swelter.e: From Middle English swelteren, frequentative form of Middle English swelten (“to die; faint”), from Old English sweltan (“to die”), from Proto-West Germanic *sweltan, from Proto-Germanic *sweltaną (“to die”), from Proto-Indo-European *swel- (“to smolder; burn”), equivalent to swelt + -er (frequentative suffix).

d.g: burn superficially or lightly

swinge.e: From Middle English swengen (“to strike”), from Old English swenġan (“to dash, strike; to cause to swing”), from Proto-West Germanic *swangijan (“to cause to swing”).

d.g: Alternative form of swash (“to dash or flow noisily; to splash”).
